choices.explanation: Clearing all previous comments before re-running does not prevent Claude from re-generating the same findings - it just hides the prior comments. The developer loses the history of what was already addressed, and the re-run still produces duplicate analysis.

choices.text: Switch to a higher-capability model version for re-review runs; newer models are better at inferring which issues have been resolved from inspecting the diff without needing to see the prior findings.
choices.explanation: Model capability does not substitute for explicit context about what was previously flagged. Without the prior findings in the prompt, even the most capable model has no way to know which issues are genuinely new versus which were present in a prior review round.

questions.tip: Think about what information Claude needs in its context to distinguish between issues it has already reported and issues that are genuinely new or still unresolved.
questions.explanation:
Injecting prior findings into context and instructing Claude to produce only a delta is the correct strategy for avoiding duplicate review comments.

**Why it works:** When Claude receives the previous round's findings alongside the new diff, it can compare the two and produce only issues that either did not appear before or appeared before and are not yet resolved. This makes each re-review a genuine delta rather than a full re-analysis, giving developers a clear signal of what still needs attention.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Hash-based deduplication: only catches exact text duplicates; does not improve Claude's analysis or tell it to reason about resolved issues.
- Clearing previous comments: removes useful history and does not prevent Claude from regenerating the same findings in the new run.
- Switching model versions: model capability does not give Claude knowledge of prior review findings without those findings being in context.

skills: 3.6.8: Providing existing test files in context so test generation avoids suggesting duplicate scenarios already covered by the test suite.
questions.question:
A developer asks Claude Code to generate additional test cases for a recently extended payment processing module. The team already has a comprehensive test file covering all core happy-path and error-handling scenarios for that module. After Claude generates the new tests, the developer notices that roughly half of the suggestions duplicate scenarios already present in the existing test file, requiring manual filtering before the tests can be added.

What change to the Claude Code prompt would most effectively reduce duplicate test suggestions?

choices.text: Instruct Claude in the prompt to skip any test involving payment failures, since that area is typically already covered in mature payment modules and always produces duplicates.
choices.explanation: Excluding entire topic areas based on general assumptions is too blunt. If legitimate gaps exist in error-handling coverage, this instruction would suppress useful suggestions along with the duplicates, and the assumption may not hold for this specific test suite.

choices.text: Ask Claude to generate twice as many test suggestions as needed, then manually discard any that look similar to existing tests before adding the remainder to the test file.
choices.explanation: Generating excess suggestions and filtering manually does not reduce the duplication problem at the source; it simply increases the review burden on the developer. The root cause is that Claude lacks visibility into what is already covered.

choices.text: Invoke Claude Code with the `--skip-existing-tests` flag to enable built-in deduplication, which compares generated test descriptions against the existing test file before returning suggestions.
choices.explanation: There is no `--skip-existing-tests` flag in Claude Code. Deduplication awareness must be provided through context, not through a hypothetical built-in flag.

choices.text: Include the contents of the existing test file in the prompt context so Claude can inspect which scenarios are already covered and focus its suggestions on gaps that remain untested.
choices.explanation: Providing the existing test file in context gives Claude direct visibility into what is already covered. Armed with this information, Claude can identify genuine gaps and avoid regenerating scenarios that already have test coverage, producing more targeted and useful suggestions.

questions.tip: Ask what information Claude would need to avoid suggesting scenarios it cannot currently see are already covered.
questions.explanation:
Providing existing test files in context is the correct way to prevent duplicate test suggestions.

**Why it works:** When Claude can read the existing test file, it knows which paths, edge cases, and error conditions are already covered. It can then focus exclusively on scenarios that have no equivalent coverage in the existing suite, making every generated suggestion genuinely additive.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Excluding topic areas by assumption: too broad; suppresses useful suggestions and relies on generalizations that may not match this specific suite.
- Generating excess and filtering manually: increases developer workload without addressing the root cause of Claude's lack of context.
- `--skip-existing-tests` flag: this flag does not exist; context injection is the correct mechanism.

skills: 3.6.9: Documenting testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md to improve test generation quality and reduce low-value test output.
questions.question:
A QA lead notices that test generation requests made by different engineers using Claude Code produce highly inconsistent results across the same monorepo. Some generated suites use the wrong test runner, others test trivial getter methods instead of meaningful behaviour, and several ignore the shared database fixture that the team has standardised on. Each engineer includes slightly different instructions in their prompts, leading to the inconsistency.

What is the most sustainable mechanism for ensuring every Claude Code test generation request consistently applies the team's testing standards without requiring each engineer to embed those standards in every prompt?

choices.text: Create a shared prompt template stored in the team wiki that each engineer must copy and paste into their Claude Code session before requesting test generation, ensuring the standards are always present in the prompt.
choices.explanation: A copy-paste workflow is manual and error-prone; engineers will forget to include it, use outdated versions, or modify it inconsistently. It also does not apply automatically in CI runs and requires ongoing maintenance to keep in sync with evolving standards.

choices.text: Store the testing standards as a standalone `TEST_STANDARDS.md` file in the repository and instruct engineers to reference it in their prompts using a `--include-file` flag so Claude Code loads it before responding.
choices.explanation: There is no `--include-file` flag in Claude Code's CLI. More importantly, this approach still requires each engineer to remember an extra step. The correct mechanism for automatic context loading is `CLAUDE.md`, not a separate file referenced via a hypothetical flag.

choices.text: Document the testing standards, approved fixture names, and valuable test criteria in the project's `CLAUDE.md` file; Claude Code reads it automatically on every invocation, applying the documented constraints without any additional steps from individual team members.
choices.explanation: `CLAUDE.md` is part of Claude Code's memory system and is loaded at the start of every session, including CI runs. By placing testing standards there once, the team ensures that every engineer's and every pipeline's test generation request is automatically grounded in the same requirements without any per-prompt overhead.

choices.text: Configure a fixed system prompt through the Claude API's system parameter that encodes the testing standards, making them apply to all API-level requests while leaving Claude Code interactive sessions to rely on individual prompt discipline.
choices.explanation: A system prompt configured at the API level applies only to direct API calls, not to Claude Code CLI sessions which have their own invocation path. This approach also splits the source of truth for standards across two mechanisms, making them harder to maintain consistently.

questions.tip: Identify the mechanism in Claude Code's memory system that loads project context automatically on every invocation, eliminating per-engineer prompt discipline requirements.
questions.explanation:
Documenting testing standards in `CLAUDE.md` is the most sustainable approach because it applies automatically and universally.

**Why it works:** `CLAUDE.md` is part of Claude Code's built-in memory system. It is loaded at the start of every session - both interactive and CI - without any extra CLI arguments or engineer action. By placing testing standards, fixture names, and valuable test criteria in `CLAUDE.md` once, the team ensures consistent, high-quality test generation across every engineer and every pipeline run.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Shared prompt template in wiki: manual and error-prone; engineers forget, use stale versions, and the approach does not work automatically in CI.
- `--include-file` flag with `TEST_STANDARDS.md`: no such flag exists; standards must be in `CLAUDE.md` for automatic loading.
- API-level system prompt: applies only to direct API calls, not to Claude Code CLI sessions, and splits the standards across two mechanisms.

skills: 4.1.1: Understanding the importance of explicit criteria over vague instructions (for example, "flag comments only when claimed behavior contradicts actual code behavior" vs "check that comments are accurate").
questions.question:
A team uses Claude to audit Python function documentation for accuracy. Their prompt instructs Claude to "check that comments are accurate," but reviewers notice Claude flags many correct comments as inaccurate, creating excessive noise in the review pipeline.

Which revised instruction is most likely to improve review precision?

choices.text: Audit each function's documentation carefully and flag comments that appear inaccurate or misleading based on your understanding of the code, paying special attention to return values, side effects, and exception behavior.
choices.explanation: "Appear inaccurate" and "your understanding" leave the threshold entirely up to Claude's interpretation, preserving the same inconsistency as the original instruction.

choices.text: Apply stricter accuracy standards by only flagging comments when you are highly confident an error exists, avoiding any flag that could be considered subjective or dependent on broader codebase context.
choices.explanation: "Highly confident" is a confidence-based filter, not a categorical criterion. Without a concrete definition of accuracy failure, Claude still applies arbitrary and inconsistent thresholds.

choices.text: Flag a comment only when the behavior it describes cannot be reconciled with what the code actually executes.
choices.explanation: This criterion is explicit and verifiable: it grounds the flag decision in a concrete, binary check - does the code contradict the comment? - rather than in Claude's subjective confidence.

choices.text: Evaluate whether each comment could mislead a developer unfamiliar with the codebase, including comments that are technically correct but potentially confusing in the context of the broader module structure.
choices.explanation: Usefulness to an unfamiliar developer is a reader-dependent and context-sensitive standard, introducing more interpretation space rather than reducing it.

questions.tip: Consider which instruction gives Claude an observable, binary test it can apply consistently rather than asking it to estimate accuracy or confidence.
questions.explanation:
Explicit criteria ground Claude's evaluation in a concrete, verifiable condition - does the code contradict the comment? Vague instructions like "check accuracy" leave Claude to define its own threshold, which varies unpredictably across runs.

**Why it works:** "Cannot be reconciled with what the code actually executes" gives Claude a stable binary check that does not depend on confidence scoring or reader simulation.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: "Appear inaccurate" is still vague - Claude must decide what appearance of inaccuracy means.
- Distractor B: "Highly confident" is a confidence filter, not a categorical rule - it preserves the same inconsistency.
- Distractor D: Simulating an unfamiliar reader is a subjective, context-dependent standard that expands rather than constrains the interpretation space.

skills: 4.1.2: Understanding how general instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" fail to improve precision compared to specific categorical criteria.
questions.question:
A security team deploys Claude for automated vulnerability scanning with the instruction "only report high-confidence findings" added to the system prompt to reduce alert noise. After two weeks, developers report that the false positive rate has not meaningfully improved.

What is the most accurate explanation for why this instruction failed?

choices.text: Claude interprets "high-confidence" as a directive to suppress its internal uncertainty markers, causing it to present all findings as definitive regardless of actual certainty, which paradoxically surfaces more marginal issues than before.
choices.explanation: Claude does not have an internal confidence-suppression mode triggered by such phrasing. This mischaracterizes how Claude processes confidence-related language in instructions.

choices.text: "High-confidence" is undefined relative to any specific vulnerability category, so Claude applies an inconsistent and unverifiable interpretation of confidence that varies by issue type and produces the same erratic filtering as the original prompt.
choices.explanation: Without a concrete per-category definition - such as "flag SQL injection only when unvalidated input directly reaches a database call" - Claude cannot apply a stable threshold and falls back to its own shifting judgment.

choices.text: The instruction reduces Claude's sensitivity uniformly across all vulnerability categories, correctly suppressing low-severity style issues but inadvertently filtering out genuine critical vulnerabilities that the original prompt would have surfaced.
choices.explanation: Confidence-based instructions do not produce reliable uniform sensitivity reduction. The actual effect is inconsistent because "confidence" has no defined meaning per category, and critical issues are not systematically suppressed.

choices.text: Claude applies the confidence filter only to the first few vulnerability categories encountered in the prompt due to positional attention constraints, leaving later categories evaluated at the original unfiltered threshold.
choices.explanation: Claude does not apply positional attention decay to instructions in this way. This fabricates a model behavior that is not related to the actual failure of vague confidence-based filtering.

questions.tip: Think about what concrete information Claude needs to apply a filter consistently - and whether "high-confidence" provides that information per category.
questions.explanation:
Instructions like "only report high-confidence findings" ask Claude to evaluate its own certainty, but without defining what confidence means for each specific vulnerability type, Claude cannot apply a consistent threshold across categories.

**Why it works:** The correct answer identifies the root failure: "high-confidence" is unanchored to any category-specific criterion, so Claude interprets it differently for each issue type.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: Claude does not suppress uncertainty markers in response to such instructions; this invents a false internal mechanism.
- Distractor C: Uniform sensitivity reduction is not the observed behavior - inconsistency is, because confidence means different things per category.
- Distractor D: Positional attention decay of this kind is not a real Claude behavior.

skills: 4.1.3: Understanding the impact of false positive rates on developer trust: high false positive categories undermine confidence in accurate categories.
questions.question:
A platform team deploys Claude for automated pull request review across three categories: security vulnerabilities, logic bugs, and code style. Security and logic bug findings are highly accurate, but the style category produces a large proportion of false positives. Two weeks after deployment, developers report that they have stopped reading review reports entirely.

What is the most likely explanation for this outcome?

choices.text: Developers become overwhelmed by the sheer volume of correct security and logic findings, even though each individual finding is accurate, causing review fatigue unrelated to the false positive rate in the style category.
choices.explanation: The scenario attributes disengagement specifically to false positives in one category, not to the total volume of correct findings in others. Review fatigue from accurate findings is a separate problem not described here.

choices.text: Developers distrust automated code review tools on principle regardless of per-category accuracy, and the style false positives simply provide a visible justification when declining to engage, meaning the root cause is organizational rather than technical.
choices.explanation: This attributes rejection to a pre-existing cultural bias rather than to the measurable contamination effect that false positives in one category have on perceived reliability across all categories.

choices.text: Security and logic bug category recommendations occasionally conflict with each other's findings, creating inconsistencies that undermine developer confidence across the entire report independently of what the style category produces.
choices.explanation: The scenario does not describe conflict between categories. The disengagement is tied specifically to false positives in the style category affecting trust in the complete report.

choices.text: The high false positive rate in the style category erodes trust in the entire review output, causing developers to discount all findings - including accurate security and logic bug reports - because they cannot efficiently distinguish reliable from unreliable signals.
choices.explanation: When one category generates persistent false positives, developers cannot selectively trust other categories without additional filtering effort. The cognitive overhead of separating noise from signal causes wholesale disengagement.

questions.tip: Consider how trust operates across a multi-category output - does a noisy category affect how developers perceive reliable categories in the same report?
questions.explanation:
A high false positive rate in any single category contaminates developer trust across the entire review output. Rather than investing effort to filter which findings are reliable, developers disengage from the report altogether.

**Why it works:** Noise in one category makes the overall signal-to-noise ratio unacceptable. Developers cannot selectively rely on other categories without manually auditing the full report.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: Volume of correct findings is not the described problem; the trigger is false positives in one category.
- Distractor B: Pre-existing cultural distrust does not explain why accurate categories also lose credibility after deployment.
- Distractor C: Inter-category conflict is not described and represents a different failure mode entirely.

skills: 4.1.4: Writing specific review criteria that define which issues to report (bugs, security) versus skip (minor style, local patterns) rather than relying on confidence-based filtering.
questions.question:
An engineering team uses Claude to review pull requests and wants to ensure only actionable findings reach developers. They are choosing between two approaches: appending "only report issues you are highly confident about" to the prompt, or rewriting the criteria to specify exactly which issue types to include and which to skip.

Why should the team prefer explicit categorical criteria over the confidence-based instruction?

choices.text: Explicit categorical criteria define which issue types to report - such as null-dereference bugs and missing authorization checks - and which to skip - such as single-variable naming inconsistencies - giving Claude a stable, auditable filter rather than a subjective confidence threshold that varies across category types.
choices.explanation: Categorical criteria anchor the filter to specific, named issue types with defined inclusion and exclusion rules, removing the ambiguity that confidence-based instructions cannot resolve.

choices.text: Confidence-based filtering is effective for reducing false positives in well-understood vulnerability categories but introduces selection bias in novel issue types, so the two approaches should be combined by applying category-specific confidence thresholds alongside explicit inclusion rules for the best precision.
choices.explanation: Combining confidence thresholds with categorical rules adds complexity without resolving the core problem. Confidence-based filtering remains undefined and inconsistent even when applied on a per-category basis.

choices.text: Explicit categorical criteria are appropriate for codebases with a small number of known issue types, but for large codebases with many potential patterns, confidence-based filtering scales better because it adapts dynamically without requiring the criteria list to be updated as the codebase evolves.
choices.explanation: Categorical criteria can describe broad classes of issues rather than individual named patterns, so scale is not a meaningful limitation. Confidence filtering does not reliably adapt to new patterns either.

choices.text: Confidence-based filtering is insufficient for known issue types where Claude has reliable training signal, but it is more accurate than categorical criteria for novel vulnerability patterns that fall outside any explicitly listed category, so teams should use categorical criteria only for the former and confidence filtering for the latter.
choices.explanation: Novel patterns are precisely where confidence-based filtering is least reliable, since Claude has no defined reference for what "confidence" means for a pattern it has not been given criteria for.

questions.tip: Think about what information Claude needs to apply a filter consistently - can it determine what 'highly confident' means without a concrete category definition?
questions.explanation:
Confidence-based instructions ask Claude to evaluate its own certainty without providing a reference point. Categorical criteria replace that judgment call with a concrete, auditable list of what to include and exclude.

**Why it works:** Specifying named issue types to report and to skip gives Claude a deterministic filter that can be inspected, tested, and refined independently of Claude's internal confidence estimation.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor B: Combining both approaches does not resolve the fundamental ambiguity in confidence-based filtering.
- Distractor C: Scale is not a limiting factor for well-written categorical criteria, which can describe broad issue classes.
- Distractor D: Confidence filtering is least reliable for novel patterns, making it inappropriate exactly where it is claimed to be superior.

skills: 4.1.5: Temporarily disabling high false-positive categories to restore developer trust while improving prompts for those categories.
questions.question:
A platform team runs an automated review pipeline with three categories: security issues, deprecated API usage, and formatting inconsistencies. Developers have stopped reading reports because the formatting category generates a high rate of false positives. The team wants to restore developer trust quickly while they separately refine the formatting prompt.

What is the most appropriate short-term action?

choices.text: Add a disclaimer section to each report that identifies which categories have known accuracy issues and instructs developers to manually validate formatting findings before acting on them, while keeping all three categories active to preserve full issue coverage during the refinement period.
choices.explanation: Requiring developers to manually validate the noisy category preserves the burden of filtering unreliable output, which is the root cause of disengagement. Disclaimers do not restore trust.

choices.text: Merge the formatting and security categories into a combined review pass so that Claude can use security issue context to disambiguate borderline formatting findings, reducing the false positive rate through cross-category reasoning without removing any output from the pipeline.
choices.explanation: Merging unrelated categories adds complexity and may degrade security accuracy. It does not address the formatting prompt deficiency and introduces new opportunities for misclassification.

choices.text: Remove the formatting category from the pipeline until the prompt for that category is refined and validated, allowing developers to trust the security and deprecated API signals without noise from the unreliable category.
choices.explanation: Temporarily removing the noisy category eliminates the source of disengagement immediately, allowing developers to reengage with the accurate categories while the team improves the formatting prompt in isolation.

choices.text: Move all formatting findings to a separate lower-priority section of the report so developers can choose to ignore them while still receiving security and deprecated API findings in the main section, preserving full pipeline output without requiring any prompt changes in the short term.
choices.explanation: Segregating findings in a lower-priority section does not reduce the cognitive burden of evaluating the noisy category. Developers must still determine which section to trust, maintaining the same disengagement dynamic.

questions.tip: Consider which action immediately removes the source of noise at its origin rather than adding another layer for developers to manage.
questions.explanation:
When one category generates persistently high false positives, the fastest way to restore developer trust is to disable that category until its prompt is improved. Developers can immediately rely on the remaining accurate signals.

**Why it works:** Removing the problematic category eliminates noise at the source, allowing the team to refine the formatting prompt independently without degrading trust in the other categories.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: Disclaimers shift the filtering burden to developers rather than removing the noisy output.
- Distractor B: Merging categories adds complexity and does not address the root prompt deficiency.
- Distractor D: Segregating lower-priority findings still requires developers to decide what to trust.

skills: 4.1.6: Defining explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each severity level to achieve consistent classification.
questions.question:
A team builds an automated code review tool using Claude and finds that severity labels - critical, high, medium, and low - are applied inconsistently across similar issues, making severity-based triage unreliable.

Which prompt modification is most effective for achieving consistent severity classification?

choices.text: Replace the four-level severity scale with a binary report-or-suppress decision, and have the consuming system derive severity from issue category and file location, removing the classification responsibility from Claude entirely to eliminate ambiguity at the model level.
choices.explanation: Externalizing severity classification does not solve the problem if the external mapping rules are similarly vague. It relocates the inconsistency rather than resolving it.

choices.text: Define each severity level with a precise observable characteristic anchored to a concrete illustrative pattern - for example, specifying that critical means unvalidated external input reaching a database query without parameterization - so Claude can compare each new issue against a clear reference template.
choices.explanation: Concrete illustrative patterns anchor each severity level to a verifiable code characteristic, reducing interpretation variance by giving Claude a stable reference example to match against.

choices.text: Instruct Claude to assign severity based on estimated business impact, using qualitative descriptions such as critical for potential production outages and high for possible data exposure, relying on Claude's general contextual knowledge of software risk to produce consistent labels.
choices.explanation: Business impact descriptions are qualitative and context-dependent. Claude's contextual risk knowledge does not produce the stable, observable criteria needed for consistent classification across independently reviewed issues.

choices.text: Add a second Claude call that re-classifies the initial review findings using a two-field impact-and-likelihood schema, then derives the final severity label programmatically by combining the two scores, separating the classification step from the initial review to improve consistency.
choices.explanation: Adding a second classification pass does not help if the severity definitions in that pass are also vague. The underlying problem is the absence of concrete criteria, not the number of passes.

questions.tip: Think about what makes a severity definition stable enough for Claude to assign the same label to two structurally similar issues reviewed in separate calls.
questions.explanation:
Consistent severity classification requires that each level be defined by observable, verifiable characteristics with a concrete reference pattern. Without such anchors, Claude applies severity based on contextual judgment that shifts across runs.

**Why it works:** Anchoring each level to an illustrative code pattern gives Claude a concrete comparison target, reducing the interpretation variance that causes inconsistent labeling.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: A binary decision externalizes the problem without providing concrete severity criteria.
- Distractor C: Business impact descriptions remain qualitative and context-dependent, producing the same inconsistency.
- Distractor D: A second classification pass inherits the same vague criteria unless those criteria are made concrete.

skills: 4.2.1: Understanding few-shot examples as the most effective technique for achieving consistently formatted, actionable output when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results.
questions.question:
A developer has written detailed formatting instructions for a Claude-powered bug report generator, specifying a required output layout with named fields. After extensive prompt iteration, the output format still varies between runs - sometimes omitting fields, sometimes reordering sections.

What is the most effective next intervention?

choices.text: Rewrite the formatting instructions with additional specificity - including character limits, capitalization requirements, and explicit descriptions of acceptable and unacceptable values per field - so Claude has a more complete rule set to draw on when constructing the output layout.
choices.explanation: Adding more detailed instructions continues the strategy that has already failed. Increasing instruction specificity does not resolve inconsistencies that detailed descriptions alone cannot prevent.

choices.text: Reduce the `temperature` setting to make Claude's output more deterministic, on the basis that stochastic sampling is the primary source of the field-level variation observed across runs.
choices.explanation: Format inconsistency in structured output is rarely caused by temperature. Reducing `temperature` affects token sampling randomness but does not teach Claude the desired layout pattern.

choices.text: Split the task into two separate Claude calls - one to identify bugs and one to format the discovered list - so that the formatting call receives clean structured input and can apply layout rules without the complexity introduced by simultaneous bug detection.
choices.explanation: Task splitting may reduce per-call complexity but does not guarantee consistent formatting. The formatting call still lacks a concrete demonstration of the desired structure.

choices.text: Add 2-4 few-shot examples that demonstrate complete, correctly formatted bug reports with all required fields populated in the correct layout.
choices.explanation: Few-shot examples give Claude a direct demonstration of the desired format. When instructions alone produce inconsistent output, concrete examples communicate the pattern in a form that Claude can generalize reliably.

questions.tip: When detailed instructions have been exhausted without resolving inconsistency, consider what technique communicates the desired pattern more directly than written rules.
questions.explanation:
Detailed instructions describe the desired output abstractly. When Claude cannot reliably infer the exact layout from descriptions alone, few-shot examples provide a direct demonstration that anchors the formatting pattern.

**Why it works:** Completed examples allow Claude to extract the layout from concrete instances rather than from abstract rules, which is more effective when instructions alone produce variance.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: More instructions continue the approach that failed - the problem is that description alone is insufficient.
- Distractor B: Reducing `temperature` addresses sampling variance, not formatting knowledge.
- Distractor C: Task splitting reduces context complexity but still doesn't provide the formatting demonstration Claude needs.

skills: 4.2.2: Understanding the role of few-shot examples in demonstrating ambiguous-case handling (for example, tool selection for ambiguous requests, branch-level test coverage gaps).
questions.question:
A developer builds a routing agent that uses Claude to select among three tools: a cached database lookup, a live web search, and a local calculation engine. Requests with clear intent route correctly, but phrasing that could be satisfied by either the database or the web search produces inconsistent tool selection across runs.

What is the most targeted solution for improving routing consistency specifically on ambiguous inputs?

choices.text: Add few-shot examples that include ambiguous inputs alongside the chosen tool and an inline rationale explaining why that option was selected over the plausible alternative, so Claude can generalize the decision rule to novel ambiguous phrasings rather than matching only listed examples.
choices.explanation: Demonstrating the decision with explicit reasoning teaches Claude the priority criterion - for example, prefer the database for latency when both tools could satisfy the request - in a form it can generalize to new phrasing.

choices.text: Expand each tool's description to enumerate every foreseeable scenario in which it should be preferred over the alternatives, covering the complete space of ambiguous inputs so Claude can match each incoming request against the documented rules without requiring demonstration examples.
choices.explanation: Enumerating every scenario is infeasible for open-ended natural language inputs, and descriptive rules cannot anticipate novel phrasings that don't match any enumerated case.

choices.text: Add a pre-classification step that uses a second Claude call to label each request as clear or ambiguous before routing, then apply a stricter rule-based decision tree for requests labeled ambiguous to isolate and simplify the tool-selection logic for that path.
choices.explanation: Pre-classification adds latency and complexity without teaching Claude the resolution rule for ambiguous cases. The stricter rules face the same tool-selection inconsistency unless examples are provided.

choices.text: Reduce the tool set from three to two by merging the cached database lookup and live web search into a single retrieval tool, eliminating the routing category that causes ambiguity without needing to teach Claude the distinction between the two retrieval modes.
choices.explanation: Merging tools removes architectural flexibility and may degrade performance for clear-cut cases. It resolves the symptom by eliminating the distinction rather than teaching the priority rule.

questions.tip: Think about how demonstrating the decision logic for edge cases differs from enumerating rules - and which approach generalizes to novel phrasing.
questions.explanation:
Few-shot examples for ambiguous cases teach Claude the priority criterion by showing the reasoning alongside the chosen action, allowing generalization to novel phrasings rather than requiring every possible input to be enumerated.

**Why it works:** Including the rationale communicates *why* one option was preferred, giving Claude a generalizable decision rule that applies to cases not shown in the examples.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor B: Enumerating every scenario is infeasible and cannot cover novel phrasing in natural language.
- Distractor C: Pre-classification adds complexity without providing the resolution logic needed for consistency.
- Distractor D: Merging tools avoids the problem instead of solving it and sacrifices architectural flexibility.

skills: 4.2.3: Understanding how few-shot examples enable the model to generalize judgment to novel patterns rather than matching only pre-specified cases.
questions.question:
A team builds an invoice classification pipeline using Claude with explicit rules covering five known invoice categories. Claude classifies those five categories accurately, but a new invoice type - consulting retainer - arrives that matches none of the written rules and is consistently misclassified.

Why do few-shot examples help Claude handle the new category correctly, even without a rule explicitly covering it?

choices.text: Few-shot examples communicate the underlying distinguishing criteria - what observable characteristics separate one category from another - allowing Claude to apply that judgment to patterns not explicitly listed rather than matching only against named cases.
choices.explanation: By demonstrating how category boundaries are drawn, examples teach Claude the evaluation logic itself, which can then be applied to novel patterns using the same underlying criteria.

choices.text: Few-shot examples compress categorical knowledge into token-efficient demonstrations, giving Claude access to a broader effective rule set than an equivalent number of tokens spent on written instructions, enabling it to cover more category variants within the same context window.
choices.explanation: Token efficiency is not the mechanism that enables generalization. Examples work because they demonstrate judgment criteria, not because they are more token-efficient representations of the same rules.

choices.text: Few-shot examples cause Claude to enter a more flexible internal processing mode during classification, reducing its sensitivity to distribution shift and making it better suited to handle out-of-distribution inputs than instruction-based prompts.
choices.explanation: Claude does not switch to a different internal processing mode based on example presence. This mischaracterizes how few-shot prompting interacts with model behavior.

choices.text: Few-shot examples create an implicit lookup table that Claude extends to novel inputs using nearest-neighbor similarity, assigning unlisted categories to the closest demonstrated class based on surface-level textual overlap with example invoice text.
choices.explanation: Few-shot prompting works by communicating judgment criteria, not by performing surface-level similarity matching against a lookup table. Nearest-neighbor retrieval describes a different mechanism entirely.

questions.tip: Consider what information a few-shot example conveys beyond just the answer - and what that allows Claude to do with inputs it has never seen.
questions.explanation:
Few-shot examples demonstrate the criteria used to draw category boundaries. Claude can apply those same criteria to a novel pattern even when no explicit rule covers it, because the examples teach the evaluation logic rather than a lookup table.

**Why it works:** Examples communicate the underlying judgment - what makes one invoice type different from another - enabling Claude to extend that reasoning to new cases using the same principles.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor B: Token efficiency is a secondary property of examples; the generalization mechanism is the transfer of judgment criteria, not context-window packing.
- Distractor C: Claude does not switch processing modes based on example presence.
- Distractor D: Nearest-neighbor text matching is a different technique; few-shot examples convey decision logic, not similarity scores.

skills: 4.2.4: Understanding the effectiveness of few-shot examples for reducing hallucination in extraction tasks (for example, handling informal measurements, varied document structures).
questions.question:
A research team uses Claude to extract dosage values from clinical trial documents. Some documents express dosages informally - for example, "roughly 200mg taken twice daily" - instead of using standard notation, and Claude frequently returns null values or substitutes plausible-sounding but incorrect numbers for these fields.

What is the most effective technique for reducing null and incorrect extractions from informally expressed dosage values?

choices.text: Add a comprehensive normalization specification to the system prompt that enumerates all known informal expression patterns and maps each to a canonical form, giving Claude explicit transformation rules to apply whenever it encounters non-standard dosage notation.
choices.explanation: Enumerating all informal patterns is infeasible given the variety of natural language expression. A specification also cannot anticipate phrasings not previously encountered, leaving gaps that produce the same extraction failures.

choices.text: Provide few-shot examples that include documents containing informally expressed dosages alongside the correct extracted values for those fields, showing Claude how to interpret non-standard notation and populate required fields accurately.
choices.explanation: Concrete examples demonstrate how to bridge informal expressions to structured field values, reducing hallucination by giving Claude a direct reference for how to handle exactly the challenging format variant it sees in production.

choices.text: Switch to a two-pass architecture where the first call extracts all text passages mentioning dosages and the second call normalizes them, reducing hallucination risk by isolating normalization from extraction so each call has a simpler, more constrained task.
choices.explanation: Task decomposition can help with complexity, but without examples showing how to interpret informal notation, the normalization call still lacks the guidance needed to avoid null or fabricated values.

choices.text: Mark dosage fields as optional in the extraction schema so Claude can return null without error when it encounters informal notation, and implement a separate flagging step that identifies all null-value outputs for downstream manual review rather than attempting automated extraction.
choices.explanation: Making fields optional accepts null as a valid outcome rather than resolving the extraction failure. This shifts work to manual review instead of improving Claude's ability to handle informal expressions.

questions.tip: Consider which approach directly demonstrates to Claude how informal expressions map to required field values, rather than adding more rules or restructuring the task.
questions.explanation:
Few-shot examples are particularly effective at reducing hallucination in extraction tasks because they show Claude exactly how to translate challenging format variants - such as informal measurements - into the required structured field values.

**Why it works:** Concrete demonstrations anchor Claude's extraction behavior to observable source text, reducing the tendency to fabricate plausible values when the format is unfamiliar.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: Enumerating all informal patterns is infeasible and cannot cover novel phrasing not in the specification.
- Distractor C: Two-pass decomposition helps with complexity but doesn't provide the format-interpretation guidance that examples do.
- Distractor D: Making fields optional accepts failure as a valid outcome rather than resolving it.

skills: 4.2.5: Creating 2-4 targeted few-shot examples for ambiguous scenarios that show reasoning for why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives.
questions.question:
A developer builds a test coverage analysis tool using Claude that must decide whether a missing branch represents a reportable gap or an acceptable omission - for example, an error-propagation path intentionally left to bubble up. Inconsistent decisions on borderline cases have made the tool's output unreliable.

Which approach is most effective for improving decision consistency on borderline cases?

choices.text: Write a comprehensive specification that enumerates every known class of acceptable omission - unreachable branches, error propagation paths, intentionally untested negative scenarios, platform-specific branches - so Claude can check each borderline case against a complete exclusion list before deciding.
choices.explanation: A comprehensive exclusion list cannot cover all borderline patterns that arise in practice. Novel cases that don't match any enumerated class still produce the same inconsistency.

choices.text: Remove the acceptable-omission category entirely and instruct Claude to flag all missing branches as gaps, then apply a post-processing rule set to filter out acceptable omissions programmatically, moving the ambiguous judgment out of the Claude prompt and into deterministic code.
choices.explanation: Post-processing rules face the same borderline-case problem as the Claude prompt unless they are also based on concrete criteria. Moving the problem downstream does not resolve it.

choices.text: Add a pre-classification call that determines whether a missing branch belongs to an error-handling path before routing it to separate prompts for error-path and non-error-path assessment, reducing the judgment complexity per call by narrowing each sub-prompt's scope.
choices.explanation: Pre-classification adds latency and requires its own borderline handling. The error-path vs. non-error-path boundary is itself ambiguous in practice, and separate prompts still face inconsistency without examples.

choices.text: Create 2-4 few-shot examples that each present a borderline missing branch alongside the chosen decision and a brief rationale explaining why the case was classified as a reportable gap or an acceptable omission.
choices.explanation: Targeted examples with explicit reasoning teach Claude the evaluation criteria for borderline cases in a form it can generalize to novel patterns, directly addressing the inconsistency on ambiguous inputs.

questions.tip: Think about what information Claude needs to resolve ambiguous cases consistently - and whether enumeration or demonstration is more effective for that purpose.
questions.explanation:
For borderline cases that do not fit neatly into any explicit rule, few-shot examples with visible rationale are the most effective technique. They teach Claude the decision criteria in a form that generalizes to novel ambiguous patterns.

**Why it works:** Including the reasoning behind each borderline decision communicates the evaluation logic, not just the answer, allowing Claude to apply the same judgment to cases not covered by the examples.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: Enumerating exclusion classes cannot cover all future borderline patterns not already identified.
- Distractor B: Post-processing rules inherit the same borderline-case ambiguity unless backed by concrete criteria.
- Distractor C: Pre-classification adds overhead without providing the decision logic needed for consistency.

skills: 4.2.6: Including few-shot examples that demonstrate specific desired output format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix) to achieve consistency.
questions.question:
A team uses Claude to generate structured code review findings with four required fields: issue location, issue description, severity, and suggested fix. Despite formatting instructions specifying each field, outputs frequently omit the suggested fix or place it in the wrong position.

Which addition to the prompt most reliably resolves the format inconsistency?

choices.text: Include 2-3 complete examples of correctly formatted findings - each showing all four required fields populated in the correct sequence - so Claude has a direct demonstration of the desired structure to replicate rather than inferring it from field descriptions.
choices.explanation: Demonstrated complete examples anchor the output structure concretely. Claude can extract the formatting pattern from finished instances more reliably than from abstract field-by-field descriptions.

choices.text: Add explicit field-level formatting rules that specify the exact label, delimiter, and structure expected for each of the four fields, and append a reminder at the end of the prompt that all four fields are required and must appear in the specified sequence on every finding.
choices.explanation: Adding more explicit rules continues the strategy that has already produced inconsistent output. Descriptive rules alone have not resolved the format variance, and adding more of them is unlikely to change the outcome.

choices.text: Move the output format specification to a separate system message and reserve the human turn for the code being reviewed, isolating formatting instructions from content to reduce the likelihood that long code inputs displace the format rules from Claude's effective attention.
choices.explanation: Placement of format instructions can affect their salience, but this does not substitute for concrete demonstrations. Claude still lacks a completed example of the four-field structure.

choices.text: Switch from free-text output to a tool-use extraction model by defining a JSON schema with the four required fields as required properties, so Claude's output is structurally constrained by the schema and the suggested fix field cannot be omitted or placed out of sequence.
choices.explanation: Switching to tool use is a valid architectural change but represents a larger redesign than necessary when the problem can be solved by adding few-shot examples to the existing prompt structure.

questions.tip: Consider what form of guidance gives Claude a direct, complete reference for the target structure rather than asking it to infer the layout from descriptions.
questions.explanation:
Few-shot examples showing complete, correctly formatted findings give Claude a direct reference for the desired output structure. When formatting instructions alone produce inconsistent output, demonstrations are the most effective fix.

**Why it works:** Completed examples allow Claude to learn the four-field format from finished instances, including the correct order and population of each field, rather than from abstract descriptions.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor B: More explicit rules continue the strategy that has already failed - the problem is that descriptions alone are insufficient.
- Distractor C: Prompt placement can affect salience but is not a substitute for concrete demonstrations.
- Distractor D: Tool use is a valid alternative but is a larger architectural change than adding examples to the existing prompt.

skills: 4.2.7: Providing few-shot examples distinguishing acceptable code patterns from genuine issues to reduce false positives while enabling generalization.
questions.question:
A team deploys Claude for automated security review and notices a high false positive rate for one specific pattern: methods that contain multiple sequential data-access calls. These are flagged as logic errors, but many are intentional and accepted patterns in the organization's codebase.

What is the most effective way to teach Claude to distinguish this acceptable pattern from genuine logic errors without eliminating detection of real issues?

choices.text: Add an explicit named exclusion rule to the prompt listing multi-access methods as an acceptable pattern to skip, alongside any other known acceptable patterns, so Claude has a documented suppression list to consult during review.
choices.explanation: A named exclusion list suppresses the entire pattern class rather than teaching Claude the distinguishing characteristics. It also cannot generalize to novel variations of the acceptable pattern not already named in the list.

choices.text: Narrow the review scope to methods below a defined length threshold so that the flagged pattern - which occurs primarily in longer methods - falls outside the reviewed set, reducing false positives by restricting input coverage rather than improving the detection logic.
choices.explanation: Narrowing scope by length threshold is a blunt suppression that also excludes real logic errors in longer methods. It reduces false positives at the cost of detection coverage for genuine issues.

choices.text: Add few-shot examples that pair the acceptable multi-access pattern with a non-issue label alongside examples of genuine logic errors in structurally similar methods, so Claude can learn the observable characteristics that distinguish the two rather than simply suppressing a named pattern.
choices.explanation: Contrasting examples teach Claude the distinguishing criteria between acceptable and problematic instances, enabling it to generalize that distinction to novel structural variants not shown in the examples.

choices.text: Add a second Claude call that re-examines flagged items against a stricter verification prompt that explicitly defines what constitutes a genuine logic error versus a recognized acceptable pattern, using a two-pass architecture to separate detection from confirmation.
choices.explanation: A two-pass architecture can improve precision but does not resolve the root problem unless the verification pass also has concrete examples or criteria. Without demonstrations, the verification prompt faces the same false positive rate.

questions.tip: Consider which approach teaches Claude the distinguishing characteristics rather than suppressing a named pattern class entirely.
questions.explanation:
Few-shot examples that pair both acceptable and problematic instances of the same structural pattern teach Claude the observable characteristics that separate them, enabling generalization to novel variants without suppressing an entire pattern class.

**Why it works:** Contrasting labeled examples communicate the decision boundary between acceptable and genuine issues, which Claude can apply to patterns structurally similar but not identical to those shown.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: Explicit suppression lists cannot generalize to unlisted variants of the acceptable pattern.
- Distractor B: Narrowing scope by length reduces coverage of real issues alongside false positives.
- Distractor D: A second verification pass inherits the same discrimination problem without concrete examples or criteria.

skills: 4.2.8: Using few-shot examples to demonstrate correct handling of varied document structures (inline citations vs bibliographies, methodology sections vs embedded details).
questions.question:
A developer builds a research paper extraction pipeline using Claude to identify citations, methodology details, and sample sizes. Papers use varied citation formats - some embed citations inline within the text, others collect them in a separate bibliography section - and Claude consistently extracts correct results from one format but returns incomplete results from the other.

What is the most effective approach for improving extraction consistency across both citation formats?

choices.text: Add explicit instructions to the prompt that describe both citation formats and specify which document regions to scan for citations in each case, covering the complete decision tree for the two known structural variants so Claude can match each paper against the documented rules.
choices.explanation: Descriptive decision-tree instructions face the same coverage problem as other rule-based approaches: they cannot anticipate the full variety of structural combinations found in real research papers of mixed provenance.

choices.text: Include at least one few-shot example for each citation format - an inline-citation paper and a bibliography-section paper - showing the correct extraction result for each, so Claude can generalize the extraction pattern from concrete structural demonstrations.
choices.explanation: Format-specific examples give Claude a direct reference for how to locate and extract citations in each structural variant, and the demonstrated criteria generalize to papers that combine or vary both formats.

choices.text: Run two separate Claude calls using format-specific prompts - one tuned for inline citations and one for bibliography-section papers - and add an automated pre-classification step that routes each paper to the appropriate call based on the presence of a reference section header.
choices.explanation: Two-pass routing adds latency and requires a reliable pre-classification heuristic. Papers with mixed citation styles may be routed incorrectly, and format-specific prompts still lack concrete extraction demonstrations.

choices.text: Mark citation fields as optional in the extraction schema so Claude can return partial results when the document structure is ambiguous, and implement a completeness-checking step that flags papers with null citation fields for targeted manual follow-up rather than attempting automated cross-format extraction.
choices.explanation: Making fields optional accepts incomplete extraction as a valid outcome rather than improving Claude's ability to handle the structural variation. This shifts effort to manual review without resolving the extraction inconsistency.

questions.tip: Consider which approach demonstrates the extraction logic for each structural variant rather than describing it - and think about which generalizes to papers that don't fit neatly into either format.
questions.explanation:
Format-specific few-shot examples directly demonstrate how to locate and extract data from each structural variant. The criteria embodied in those examples generalize to papers that combine or vary both formats in ways not explicitly shown.

**Why it works:** Concrete examples for each citation structure give Claude a reference extraction pattern per format, enabling generalization without requiring exhaustive enumeration of all possible structural combinations.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: Descriptive rules cannot anticipate the full variety of structural combinations in real papers.
- Distractor C: Two-pass routing adds complexity and requires reliable pre-classification; mixed-format papers may be misrouted.
- Distractor D: Optional fields accept extraction failure as a valid outcome rather than resolving it.

skills: 4.2.9: Adding few-shot examples showing correct extraction from documents with varied formats to address empty/null extraction of required fields.
questions.question:
A data engineering team uses Claude to extract structured fields from medical device operator manuals. The manuals express output specifications in varied formats - ranges, single nominal values, and prose descriptions - and Claude returns null for the output specification field in approximately a third of documents.

What prompt addition most reliably reduces null extractions for the output specification field?

choices.text: Add validation instructions asking Claude to confirm that each extracted field value is explicitly stated in the document before populating it, and to output a structured error object instead of returning null when the output specification cannot be found in any standard or non-standard location.
choices.explanation: Validation instructions ask Claude to check its own work but do not provide guidance on how to locate or interpret the field in non-standard format presentations. Null extractions will persist for format variants Claude does not recognize.

choices.text: Add a verification pass using a second Claude call that receives each document alongside the initial extraction and confirms or corrects null-value fields by searching for the output specification in alternative document sections, targeting the null-return cases specifically.
choices.explanation: A verification pass can identify cases where extraction failed but still lacks guidance on how to interpret the varied format presentations. Without examples, the second call will produce the same null results for unfamiliar formats.

choices.text: Add a confidence score field alongside the output specification field, instructing Claude to return a numeric score from 0 to 1 for each extraction, and implement a post-processing threshold that routes low-confidence results to a targeted re-extraction workflow rather than accepting them as null.
choices.explanation: Confidence scoring and re-routing does not give Claude the format interpretation guidance it needs to extract the field correctly. The re-extraction workflow will produce the same null results without concrete format demonstrations.

choices.text: Add few-shot examples that each show a document excerpt expressing the output specification in a different format variant - range, nominal value, or prose - alongside the correctly extracted field value, so Claude can recognize and extract the specification from each structural presentation.
choices.explanation: Format-specific examples directly demonstrate how to locate and extract the field from each presentation variant, giving Claude concrete references for the cases that currently produce null results.

questions.tip: Consider which approach gives Claude the format recognition guidance it needs rather than adding verification layers that will face the same extraction gap.
questions.explanation:
Few-shot examples for each format variant give Claude a direct reference for locating and extracting the required field from presentations it currently misses, addressing the null-extraction problem at its source.

**Why it works:** Each example demonstrates how the output specification appears in a specific format, teaching Claude to recognize and extract values from presentations that previously returned null.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: Validation instructions do not help Claude locate the field in unfamiliar format presentations.
- Distractor B: A verification pass without format demonstrations faces the same extraction gap as the initial call.
- Distractor C: Confidence scoring and re-routing adds overhead but does not provide the format recognition guidance Claude needs.

skills: 4.3.1: Understanding tool use (tool_use) with JSON schemas as the most reliable approach for guaranteed schema-compliant structured output, eliminating JSON syntax errors.
questions.question:
A team builds a Claude-powered invoice processing pipeline that must return structured data in a strict schema. Using a prompt that instructs Claude to "respond with JSON matching this schema," they observe occasional JSON syntax errors and missing required fields that break downstream parsing.

What is the most reliable technique for guaranteeing schema-compliant output?

choices.text: Define the desired schema as a `tool_use` tool with JSON Schema input parameters, set `tool_choice` to force Claude to call that tool, and extract the structured data from the `tool_use` response block.
choices.explanation: Invoking a tool with a JSON Schema input definition forces Claude to emit a structurally valid tool call, eliminating JSON syntax errors by construction because the API validates the output before returning it.

choices.text: Add a post-processing validation step that parses Claude's JSON response, catches syntax errors, and automatically retries the full conversation with an appended error message so Claude can correct the malformed output in a follow-up turn.
choices.explanation: Retry loops can recover from some failures but do not eliminate the source of syntax errors. Each retry still relies on free-text JSON generation, which can repeat the same formatting mistakes.

choices.text: Embed the full JSON schema in the system prompt alongside a strict instruction that all responses must be valid JSON conforming to that schema, and repeat a JSON compliance reminder at the end of every human turn to reinforce the constraint across the conversation.
choices.explanation: Repeating schema instructions in text can reduce but does not eliminate JSON syntax errors or missing fields. Free-text JSON generation offers no structural guarantee comparable to tool-use enforcement.

choices.text: Set the `response_format` parameter to `json_object` in the API request so Claude emits only valid JSON without any prose, guaranteeing schema compliance and eliminating missing-field errors without requiring changes to the tool configuration.
choices.explanation: The Claude API does not have a `response_format` parameter. This option describes an OpenAI API feature that does not exist in the Anthropic API and would not be actionable.

questions.tip: Think about which approach removes the responsibility for valid JSON formatting from free-text generation entirely.
questions.explanation:
Using `tool_use` with a JSON Schema input definition is the most reliable method for guaranteed schema-compliant output because it eliminates free-text JSON generation. The API enforces structural validity before returning the response.

**Why it works:** Tool input schemas are validated by the API, so JSON syntax errors and missing required fields are impossible by construction rather than handled through retries or instructions.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor B: Retry loops can recover some failures but don't prevent the source of syntax errors in free-text generation.
- Distractor C: Instructional reinforcement reduces errors but offers no structural guarantee.
- Distractor D: `response_format` is an OpenAI API parameter; it does not exist in the Claude API.

skills: 4.3.2: Understanding the distinction between tool_choice: "auto" (model may return text instead of calling a tool), "any" (model must call a tool but can choose which), and forced tool selection (model must call a specific named tool).
questions.question:
A developer builds a document classification pipeline that may receive documents of several types. Three specialized extraction tools are defined - one per document type - and the developer needs to guarantee that Claude always calls one of them rather than returning a plain text response, but needs Claude to choose which tool is most appropriate for each document.

Which `tool_choice` setting achieves this requirement?

choices.text: Set `tool_choice` to `"auto"` so Claude can evaluate each document and choose the most contextually appropriate tool, while also retaining the ability to return a plain text response when none of the tools is a strong match for the document content.
choices.explanation: `"auto"` allows Claude to return a text response instead of calling a tool. This does not satisfy the requirement that every document must produce a structured tool call.

choices.text: Set `tool_choice` to a specific named tool using the forced selection format so Claude always calls the designated extraction tool regardless of which document type is received, guaranteeing a tool call on every request at the cost of selecting the same schema for all document types.
choices.explanation: Forced selection guarantees a tool call but locks Claude to a single tool, eliminating the ability to choose the most appropriate schema per document type - the other half of the stated requirement.

choices.text: Set `tool_choice` to `"any"` so Claude must call one of the provided tools for every document but can select which one best fits the document characteristics, guaranteeing structured output without restricting selection to a single fixed tool.
choices.explanation: `"any"` requires Claude to call a tool on every response while leaving the choice of which tool to Claude's judgment - satisfying both the structured-output guarantee and the per-document tool selection requirement.

choices.text: Consolidate the three tools into a single unified extraction schema with optional fields covering all possible attributes across all document types, then set `tool_choice` to `"auto"` so Claude calls the merged tool when it recognizes the document and returns text when it does not.
choices.explanation: Merging schemas into one tool collapses per-document-type precision into a single generalized schema, and `"auto"` still allows text responses when the document type is ambiguous - neither part of the stated requirement is met.

questions.tip: Think about which `tool_choice` value makes a tool call mandatory while still allowing Claude to pick among the available tools.
questions.explanation:
The `"any"` setting requires Claude to call one of the available tools on every response while still choosing which tool is most appropriate - combining the call guarantee of forced selection with the flexibility of `"auto"`.

**Why it works:** `tool_choice: "any"` mandates a tool call without locking the selection to a specific tool, satisfying both constraints simultaneously.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: `"auto"` allows Claude to skip tool calls entirely and return plain text, violating the guarantee requirement.
- Distractor B: Forced named-tool selection removes Claude's ability to choose the most appropriate schema per document.
- Distractor D: Merging schemas and using `"auto"` satisfies neither the call guarantee nor per-type schema selection.

skills: 4.3.3: Understanding that strict JSON schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but do not prevent semantic errors (for example, line items that don't sum to total, values in wrong fields).
questions.question:
A developer uses `tool_use` with a strict JSON schema to extract invoice data from supplier documents. After deploying to production, JSON syntax errors have been eliminated, but a small percentage of invoices are rejected by downstream validation because extracted line-item totals do not sum to the invoice total field.

What does this outcome demonstrate about the limits of schema enforcement via `tool_use`?

choices.text: The JSON schema is specified too narrowly at the field type level and should be extended with custom constraint keywords - such as arithmetic relationship validators - to enforce cross-field dependencies like the sum invariant, which would eliminate the total-mismatch errors.
choices.explanation: Standard JSON Schema does not support runtime arithmetic constraints between fields. Even extended schema keywords cannot enforce computed cross-field relationships during Claude's extraction process.

choices.text: A strict `tool_use` schema enforced via the API guarantees syntactic correctness - valid field names, required field presence, and correct data types - but does not prevent semantic errors such as extracted values placed in the wrong field or line items that do not sum to the stated total.
choices.explanation: Schema validation catches structural problems - missing fields, wrong types, invalid names - but cannot verify computed or cross-field relationships. Semantic correctness requires separate validation logic.

choices.text: The discrepancy indicates that the source supplier documents contain genuine arithmetic errors that Claude faithfully extracts into the structured output, meaning the `tool_use` schema and extraction prompt are working correctly and the downstream validator is misconfigured.
choices.explanation: While source document errors are possible, the scenario states the pipeline rejects invoices in which extracted totals don't sum correctly - the more direct explanation is that schema enforcement does not catch cross-field semantic errors.

choices.text: JSON schemas enforce structural constraints at parse time but Claude populates field values before schema validation occurs, so inserting a pre-population arithmetic-checking Claude call between extraction and schema validation would catch cross-field semantic errors before they reach the downstream system.
choices.explanation: The claim that schema validation occurs only after value population mischaracterizes the tool-use mechanism. The core issue is that schema validation checks structure, not arithmetic relationships between fields, regardless of sequencing.

questions.tip: Think about the distinction between what a JSON schema can enforce - structure - and what it cannot - computed relationships between values.
questions.explanation:
`tool_use` with JSON schemas guarantees that outputs are structurally valid: required fields are present, types are correct, and field names match. But schemas cannot verify semantic relationships such as arithmetic consistency between fields.

**Why it works:** Schema enforcement operates at the structural level. Cross-field invariants like sum consistency require separate application-layer validation logic that runs after extraction.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: Standard JSON Schema cannot enforce runtime arithmetic constraints between fields.
- Distractor C: Attributing all mismatches to source document errors ignores the structural vs. semantic distinction that the outcome actually illustrates.
- Distractor D: Mischaracterizes how `tool_use` validation works; the issue is what schemas can check, not when they run.

skills: 4.3.4: Understanding schema design considerations: required vs optional fields, enum fields with "other" + detail string patterns for extensible categories.
questions.question:
A developer is designing an extraction schema for customer support ticket classification. The schema must categorize tickets into three known types - billing, technical, and account management - but must also handle ticket types that do not fit any predefined category without causing extraction failures or forcing Claude to fabricate a category label.

Which schema design pattern most effectively handles both known and unanticipated ticket types?

choices.text: Define the category field as a free-text string without enum constraints, allowing Claude to populate it with any label, and run a post-processing normalization step that maps free-text outputs to canonical categories or flags unknowns for manual review.
choices.explanation: Removing enum constraints accepts free-text variability that makes downstream processing unpredictable. Normalization must handle an unbounded vocabulary of possible labels, introducing fragility.

choices.text: Define the category field as a required enum with exactly three values - billing, technical, and account-management - and add a downstream validation step that rejects any ticket unclassifiable within those three categories and routes it to a manual review queue.
choices.explanation: A closed enum with only the three known values forces Claude to select one even when none fits, producing misclassification. Downstream rejection does not help Claude express that the ticket is genuinely out-of-category.

choices.text: Define the category as an optional nullable field with the three known enum values, so Claude can return null when a ticket does not match any known type, and send all null-category tickets to a second Claude call with a broader, open-ended classification prompt.
choices.explanation: Using null for unknown categories is better than forced misclassification, but null is semantically ambiguous - it might mean unknown, missing, or inapplicable. A dedicated "other" value with a detail field is more expressive and informative.

choices.text: Define the category as an enum that includes the three known values plus "other", and pair it with an optional sibling detail field that Claude populates with a free-text description when the category is "other", preserving schema integrity while capturing unanticipated types gracefully.
choices.explanation: The "other" + detail pattern keeps the primary field structured and parseable while allowing Claude to express genuinely novel categories in the detail string, avoiding both forced misclassification and unstructured free-text in the category field.

questions.tip: Think about how to keep the primary classification field structured and machine-parseable while still giving Claude a way to express categories not covered by the enum.
questions.explanation:
The "other" + detail pattern preserves the structured enum field for all known categories while providing a semantically distinct escape valve for unknown types. Claude can signal that a ticket is out-of-category without fabricating a label or returning null.

**Why it works:** The enum prevents free-text contamination of the primary field, and the optional detail field captures the specific nature of the novel category for human review or downstream handling.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Distractor A: Free-text strings create an unbounded vocabulary that complicates downstream processing.
- Distractor B: A closed enum forces Claude to misclassify tickets that genuinely fall outside the known set.
- Distractor C: Null is semantically ambiguous and less informative than a dedicated "other" + detail pair.

skills: 4.3.5: Defining extraction tools with JSON schemas as input parameters and extracting structured data from the tool_use response.
questions.question:
A developer wants Claude to extract structured metadata - title, author, and publication date - from academic paper abstracts and return the data as a typed object for downstream processing.

Which implementation approach guarantees structured output and enables the application to access the extracted fields reliably?

choices.text: Define an `extract_metadata` tool with an `input_schema` specifying the required fields as typed properties, force the tool call using `tool_choice`, and read the extracted values from the `tool_use` block in Claude's response.
choices.explanation: Defining the extraction schema as a tool's `input_schema` and forcing the call ensures Claude returns the data in a structured `tool_use` block with validated field types, which the application reads directly.

choices.text: Instruct Claude in the system prompt to return the metadata as a JSON object with the required field names, and parse the response text as JSON in the application layer, catching any syntax errors that occur when Claude deviates from the specified format.
